questions.topic: 1H NMR Chemical Shift of Aromatic Protons
questions.question: In what characteristic chemical shift range do aromatic ring protons on benzene derivatives resonate in ¹H NMR?

options.label: C
options.text: Between δ 6.5 and 8.5 ppm (downfield, deshielded by aromatic ring current magnetic anisotropy).

questions.correct_answer: Between δ 6.5 and 8.5 ppm (downfield, deshielded by aromatic ring current magnetic anisotropy).
questions.explanation: Induced ring current creates an anisotropic magnetic field that reinforces B₀ outside the ring, shifting aromatic protons downfield to 6.5–8.5 ppm.

questions.question: At what diagnostic chemical shift does the formyl proton (-CHO) of an aldehyde appear in ¹H NMR?

options.label: C
options.text: At δ 9.0–10.0 ppm (highly deshielded singlet or multiplet).

questions.correct_answer: At δ 9.0–10.0 ppm (highly deshielded singlet or multiplet).
questions.explanation: Inductive electron withdrawal by oxygen combined with carbonyl magnetic anisotropy shifts the aldehyde proton far downfield to 9–10 ppm.

questions.question: Where does the acidic hydroxyl proton (-COOH) of a carboxylic acid characteristically appear in ¹H NMR?

options.label: C
options.text: Far downfield at δ 10.0–12.5 ppm as a broad singlet.

questions.correct_answer: Far downfield at δ 10.0–12.5 ppm as a broad singlet.
questions.explanation: Strong hydrogen bonding and powerful inductive deshielding shift the carboxylic acid O-H proton extremely far downfield to 10–12.5 ppm.

questions.question: What characteristic ¹H NMR multiplet pattern confirms the presence of an isolated ethyl group (-CH₂-CH₃)?

options.label: B
options.text: A 3H triplet (J ~ 7 Hz) upfield coupled to a 2H quartet (J ~ 7 Hz) downfield.

questions.correct_answer: A 3H triplet (J ~ 7 Hz) upfield coupled to a 2H quartet (J ~ 7 Hz) downfield.
questions.explanation: According to the n+1 rule, CH₃ protons split CH₂ into a quartet (3+1=4); CH₂ protons split CH₃ into a triplet (2+1=3).

questions.question: What characteristic ¹H NMR splitting pattern identifies an isolated isopropyl group [-CH(CH₃)₂]?

options.label: C
options.text: A 6H doublet coupled to a 1H septet (7 peaks, J ~ 7 Hz).

questions.correct_answer: A 6H doublet coupled to a 1H septet (7 peaks, J ~ 7 Hz).
questions.explanation: Six equivalent methyl protons split the single methine proton into a septet (6+1=7); the methine splits the methyls into a doublet (1+1=2).

questions.question: What ¹H NMR signal is the definitive diagnostic signature of an isolated tert-butyl group [-C(CH₃)₃]?

options.label: C
options.text: An intense, sharp 9H singlet at approximately δ 0.9–1.3 ppm.

questions.correct_answer: An intense, sharp 9H singlet at approximately δ 0.9–1.3 ppm.
questions.explanation: Nine chemically and magnetically equivalent protons with zero neighboring hydrogens produce an intense 9H singlet.

questions.question: In what chemical shift region do ketone and aldehyde carbonyl carbons resonate in broadband-decoupled ¹³C NMR?
questions.correct_answer: Far downfield at δ 190–220 ppm.
questions.explanation: Ketone and aldehyde carbonyl carbons are severely deshielded by the polar C=O bond, resonating far downfield at 190–220 ppm.

questions.topic: Ester and Amide 13C Carbonyl Chemical Shifts
questions.question: In what chemical shift region do ester, amide, and carboxylic acid carbonyl carbons resonate in ¹³C NMR?

options.label: A
options.text: At δ 160–185 ppm (upfield of ketones/aldehydes due to resonance lone-pair donation from heteroatoms).

questions.correct_answer: At δ 160–185 ppm (upfield of ketones/aldehydes due to resonance lone-pair donation from heteroatoms).
questions.explanation: Heteroatom lone pair resonance donation shields the carbonyl carbon relative to ketones, shifting resonance upfield to 160–185 ppm.

questions.question: How does a DEPT-90 NMR spectrum differ from a DEPT-135 NMR spectrum for an unknown hydrocarbon?

options.label: A
options.text: DEPT-90 is a proton NMR experiment.

options.label: C
options.text: DEPT-90 displays ONLY CH (methine) carbons as positive peaks; DEPT-135 displays CH and CH₃ carbons as positive peaks and CH₂ carbons as negative (inverted) peaks.

questions.correct_answer: DEPT-90 displays ONLY CH (methine) carbons as positive peaks; DEPT-135 displays CH and CH₃ carbons as positive peaks and CH₂ carbons as negative (inverted) peaks.
questions.explanation: DEPT-90 isolates CH carbons exclusively; comparing with DEPT-135 allows definitive assignment of CH₃, CH₂, and CH carbons.

options.label: A
options.text: The smallest peak in the spectrum.

options.label: B
options.text: The peak with the highest m/z value.

options.label: C
options.text: The most intense peak in the mass spectrum, arbitrarily assigned an abundance of 100%, representing the most stable and abundant fragment ion.

options.label: D
options.text: The peak corresponding to unfragmented solvent.

questions.correct_answer: The most intense peak in the mass spectrum, arbitrarily assigned an abundance of 100%, representing the most stable and abundant fragment ion.
questions.explanation: The base peak is the tallest peak (100% relative abundance), corresponding to the most thermodynamically stable fragment ion formed.
